name: Amazon EBS
summary: Network-attached virtual disks for EC2 instances, sized and tuned per volume.
intro: An EBS volume is a disk that lives on the network, not inside the server. You create it in one Availability Zone, attach it to an EC2 instance in that same zone, and the operating system sees an ordinary block device to format and mount. The volume outlives the instance, so you can detach it and attach it to another one. On current instances you can grow it, change its type or raise its performance while it stays in use.

You choose a volume type per disk. `gp3`, the general-purpose SSD, includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size, and you can pay for up to 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s on volumes up to 64 TiB. `io2` Block Express goes to 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MiB/s with average latency under 500 microseconds and 99.999% durability. The HDD types `st1` and `sc1` are cheap throughput for large sequential reads. Snapshots are incremental, store only changed blocks in S3, and can restore a volume in any zone of the Region.
strengths: Performance is set per volume, and `gp3` lets you buy IOPS and throughput separately from size
Volumes persist independently of instances and can be resized or retyped live
Incremental snapshots are cheap backups and the way to move a disk to another zone
`io2` Block Express gives sub-millisecond latency for demanding databases
limits: Tied to one Availability Zone; a zone outage takes the volume with it until you restore from a snapshot
Usually one instance at a time; Multi-Attach works only on `io1` and `io2`, and needs a cluster-aware file system
You pay for the provisioned size whether or not it’s full
`gp3` durability is 99.8–99.9% a year, and AWS doesn’t snapshot your volumes unless you set it up

story: When EC2 opened in beta in 2006, an instance’s disk belonged to that instance: terminate the instance and the data was lost. That made EC2 awkward for anything that had to keep state, such as a database.

AWS launched Elastic Block Store on 20 August 2008, nearly two years after EC2’s beta. A volume of 1 GB to 1 TB attached to one instance in one Availability Zone, was replicated automatically within that zone, and could be snapshotted to S3. It cost $0.10 per GB-month plus $0.10 per million I/O requests. Werner Vogels described block storage as the third storage pattern Amazon’s internal analysis had found, alongside key-value storage (S3) and simple structured data (SimpleDB).

The first EBS ran on hard drives that managed roughly 120–150 operations a second each, and customers sharing disks slowed each other down. Over the next decade the team, as engineer Marc Olson later recounted, retrofitted SSDs, moved storage processing off the host onto Nitro cards and wrote its own network protocol, SRD. By 2024 EBS was handling over 140 trillion operations a day.

choices.choice: On the network, not inside the server
choices.why: Keeping volumes on separate storage servers lets a disk outlive its instance and be attached to another one, which instance storage couldn’t do. Every I/O pays for a network round trip in return.

choices.choice: Replicated within one zone, with snapshots to S3
choices.why: Each volume is copied automatically inside its Availability Zone. Surviving the loss of that zone, or moving a volume to another one, goes through incremental snapshots stored in S3.
A plain block device lets the customer choose the layer above it, from a file system such as ZFS to a database that manages its own blocks.
Early users striped several volumes together to go faster. Provisioned IOPS (2012) and `gp3` (2020) let them pay for IOPS and throughput directly instead.

timeline.text: Launches on 20 August: 1 GB–1 TB volumes, snapshots stored in S3
A faulty network change in US East causes a “re-mirroring storm” outage (April)
Provisioned IOPS volumes offer up to 1,000 IOPS (July)
`gp3` decouples IOPS and throughput from size, up to 20% cheaper than `gp2`
`io2` Block Express: up to 256,000 IOPS with sub-millisecond latency (July)
`gp3` grows to 64 TiB, 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s (September)
